body: We also need better type inference because no one wants to specify all template parameters. And with current generic resolution we just should specify all paramters if only one is unknown for compiler. Thus, without [this feature](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/5023) this request seems to be quite impractical.

There's only one thing I don't like about these HKT proposals:

> 1. `T` is constrained to be a generic type definition with one type parameter.

I'm not sure I understand why HKTs would put such a limitation on `T`.  Why must it be a generic type of any specific arity, or a generic type at all, as long as it meets the other requirements of being both instantiatable and implementing `ICollection<?>`?  Wouldn't this prevent using non-generic concrete types that implement the generic collection interfaces?  What if I had a container type `class StringList : ICollection<string>`?

Maybe I'm missing something obvious/functional here?

The generic code that uses the generic wants to instantiate it, and in order to do that it needs to provide the correct number of type parameters. So the number of type parameters needs to be statically known.
@HaloFour I agree, something like partially specialized types would be a welcome addition, although now we're probably venturing into the tail end of a Zipf's distribution of feature usefulness.

Any new generic constraints should be implemented in the same place as the old generic constraints--the CLR type system--and not as a big hack inside the C# compiler.  It's important to remember that CLR does not stand for "C# Language Runtime."  If we add something as big as higher-kinded types, it should be added inside the CLR, to minimize the amount of work that the maintainers of other languages have to do in order to get up to speed on the new features.

This would likely require a new CLR major version and the addition of at least one new metadata table.  Backwards compatibility would be trivial (if your assembly doesn't have the new table(s), just don't worry about it.)  Forwards compatibility, not so much, but it would be worth the pain.  The last time we added new metadata, we were able to deal with the compatibility break just fine, and it brought the CLR into a major leap forward.  But after 12 years, the CLR 2.0 architecture is really starting to show its limitations.  If we're going to do this, we should do it right, instead of even more piling of hacks upon hacks upon hacks.

I'm going to assume you started implementing this as a type parameter constraint (`GenConstraint` I think its called in the CLI spec) - this _should work_, and is probably the most sane starting point.

I was actually thinking about something a bit more robust, like being able to encode _Kinds_ in the CLR (so we can finally talk about the type `List<>` actually has, model kinds like `* -> (* -> *) -> *`, have the CLR at runtime enforce proper kindedness of types, etc.).


Something like:

- `{type}< {type-arity} >` (e.g. `List<>`) is a "new kind" of thing, e.g. not a class, or an interface, or an object, but a "type-constructor", which of course is also a type

- This is a valid expression `IEnumerable<> enum1 = (List<>)(...)`. this is OK because type constructors are actual types (although this would be a type-level expression, which might look strange - no real analog in C#) - to be more precise, `IEnumerable<>` is a proper type

- Some type / function like ` Something<T<>>`, with `T<>` as the type parameter  cannot take a `List<string>` as a type argument, or some kind-0  / proper-type like `string` as an argument. It can only take an arity-1 type-constructor (e.g. `Task<>`), with the benefit that this can be enforced by the CLR itself (regardless of the compiler), and can be communicated/encoded across CLI languages

- Then something like `where T<> : IEnumerable<>` isn't referring to variance (that should be clear), but is instead a constraint which is constraining the type-constructor that can be accepted for `T<>`

- And we can still encode variance constraints for type-constructors as well, since there are cases where that matters (e.g. `Something<T<out _>>` or `Something<T<in _>>` for example, seems concise)


Perhaps that can all be done with `GenConstraint` and it is the best way to implement the above, but it doesn't "feel" correct. Consider this example:

```
SomeFunction<T> where T : object
// ...
SomeFunction2<T> where T : <>, object
//...
SomeFunction3<T<>> where T<> : object
```

So specifically the second case/syntax really helps highlight for me that a generic parameter of `T` and one of `T<>` are not the same thing (in fact they are not, they are not even the same _kind_ of thing). So it seems more correct to say that we need different kinds of type arguments, vs. just saying I have some type `T`, and that type is constrained to be some type-constructor with the shape `* -> *`.

In any implementation, we need to be able to model the condition that some type argument is a type constructor, and that we can constrain that type argument in various ways (sub-type/variance)...

Better would be to generalize this to: "we need a way to encode kinds in the type system" - or said another way "should `Dictionary<,>` have a type in the CTS, just like `Dictionary<A, B>` does?" - I think it should!

Any thoughts from anyone?

E.g. if I right-project a `Left<L, _>` `n` times to new types, without a bottom-type, I have to keep allocating new instances of `Left<L, n>`, v.s. just being able to reuse my initial instance of `Left<L, Nothing/absurd>`

I really liked your idea of the [Indirection Table](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/6408), but I was hoping there was something possible without adding new metadata tables (maybe there isn't).

Currently in the CLR, generic instantiations require proper types (i.e. all CLR generic parameters are instantiated to closed types). Since a type constructor necessarily has one or more type "holes", it made sense to just use `System.__Canon` as the hole type.

It still seems to me you need some type of sub-typing (which in the CLR, _is_ inheritance or interface implementation) relationship or an additional / new type in order to encode partial type application / type lambdas. And type-lambdas are "the same kind of thing" (for lack of coffee/better phrasing) as type constructors, so I think if you get one, you get both.

You'd need something like (forgive the syntax) `class Test<F<X> forAll X>`. I guess this would be fine if you enforced that HKT could only be defined on abstract classes / interfaces, and instantiations required `n` free type parameters. Seems like a workable limitation if that is the idea.

I'm trying to understand how the indirection table idea solves these issues (or what else would be needed to complete the implementation), so feedback would be appreciated.

@masaeedu 
> > As Frassle points out (and I eventually realized) partial type application of type constructors is isomorphic (maybe equivalent to?) to type-lambdas, so if you have one, you necessarily have the other...

> I'm probably not understanding what you mean by "type-lambdas", but it is possible to have a type system with type constructors and partial application of these type constructors, but without the ability to supply a "type lambda" wherever a type constructor is expected. See for example Haskell.

It seems like if you had a language where you had type lambdas and generics, but you didn't have type constructors, you could encode type constructors using type lambdas (e.g. `a => FixedGenericType[a] forAll a`).

And also if you had type constructors, but didn't have type lambdas, you could encode a type lambda as a type constructor. Further, partial application of type constructor looks like a type lambda (e.g. `a => HashTable[a, ?]`) which is then a type constructor (e.g. `HashTable[A, ?]` has the same kind as `F[?]`).

I wasn't meaning / intending to imply the two could be used interchangeably in a given type position, just that partial application of type constructors and type lambdas seem to be isomorphic. A particular type system would have to have the logic to say that you can use one in place of the other.

> And also if you had type constructors, but didn't have type lambdas, you could encode a type lambda as a type constructor

You can't do this in Haskell. For example given `Either :: * -> * -> *`, you can pass around `Either Int :: * -> *`, but there is no way to pass around `(\e -> Either e Int) :: * -> *`. The only way to deal with this is to make a different type and convert back and forth at the term level.

> Currently in the CLR, generic instantiations require proper types (i.e. all CLR generic parameters are instantiated to closed types). Since a type constructor necessarily has one or more type "holes", it made sense to just use System.__Canon as the hole type.

Yes! This is the big change that HKT adds is that now the CLR needs to be able to talk about generic instantiations that aren't full instantiated. "holes" was the name I used in my prototype. 

So normally in the CLR a Type can be a GENERICINST which has a generic type and then the types to fill it's parameters in with like ``GENERICINST List`1 int``, but with HKT you now need to be able to pass just ``List`1`` by itself as a generic parameter, but also to do things like for compose where you have 'holes' which would look something like ``GENERICINST List`1 (GENERICINST List`1 HOLE_0)`` which is like the type lambda ``x => List`1<List`1<x>>``. 

N.B. ``List`1`` that is the type token by itself would be treated the same as ``GENERICINST List`1 HOLE_0``

Now these type signatures with HOLEs can only be part of verification, no value could have these types because they're not really types they're kinds, but so are generic classes and the CLR just isn't built for this distinction.

> You'd need something like (forgive the syntax) class Test<F<X> forAll X>

That would be universals which would also be a really nice type addition to the CLR but isn't related to HKT :)

> partial application of type constructors and type lambdas seem to be isomorphic

I don't think they're strictly isomorphic, you can do more with lambda than with partial application, for example you can swap the order of the parameters:
``x => y => IDictionary<y, x>`` 
I don't think that's possible with just partial application.

> no IL or metadata changes since

Default methods on interfaces was a metadata change, as was ref structs I think. But I don't think any new tables have been added.

The really sad thing about HKT is not only does it need a new table but if you want to keep binary search working it needs to change the bit encoding of table indices as well, which there's been some strong comments made against that.

`IDictionary<?, int>` is a shorthand for `\x -> IDictionary<x, int>`, so you're effectively saying "given type lambdas, we can implement type lambdas". :)

@masaeedu - ok, how about if we define new types instead of using lambdas then?

```

```

Yes, that works. All you have to do is convert between them at the term level. So e.g. if you have `Either<E, A>`, to turn it into something that focuses on the first parameter, you need to make a different type `FlipEither<A, E>` (or something higher order), and then convert back and forth using term level functions `Either<E, A> Forward(FlipEither<A, E> e)` and `FlipEither<A, E> Backward(Either<E, A> e)`.

As you might imagine this quickly turns into a bit of a PITA.

I did say "isomorphic" not "equivalent" / "interchangeable", which does imply a mapping / reverse mapping.

Anyway - we are getting off topic..

> The really sad thing about HKT is not only does it need a new table but if you want to keep binary search working it needs to change the bit encoding of table indices as well, which there's been some strong comments made against that.

If that is the case - that's what I'll look into further when I get the time. I'm just concerned about backwards compatibility, but it was probably a pipe dream to think this could be done without some sort of breaking change...

The mapping/reverse mapping you're talking about between type systems with type lambdas and without doesn't exist. In the absence of type level lambda abstraction, the user needs to defunctionalize all of their type level programming, which is what the term level isomorphisms help us to do.

This is less expressive than having a first class lambda calculus at the type level, and makes many useful patterns impossible or extremely inconvenient (as I've learnt from painful experience). The tradeoff is that if C# ever wants to implement HM-style type inference (perhaps in support of implicits/typeclasses), those problems are undecidable once your type level language is a full blown lambda calculus.

They're distinct points in the design space, and given that this is a discussion about implementing HKT in C#, it's important to distinguish what you gain and lose with each.

I hope C# will eventually have nice solution for higher-kinded types. I'd like to share my experiments to encode HKT with generics.
https://github.com/tgrospic/object-algebras

My interest is how we can use HKT and escape know issues like difficult composition of monad transformers or free monads which requires extra structure with impact on performance.
In the repository there are two samples. One is re-implementation of [Banking sample](https://github.com/tgrospic/object-algebras/blob/8fb067b/Samples/BankingAppSample/Banking.Main/Program.cs#L58) from `language-ext` library which gave me initial inspiration (thanks Paul!). It is easier to extend both the data and the functions over data, as a solution to expression problem.
Another example is more in the functional style. [JSON parser](https://github.com/tgrospic/object-algebras/blob/37d9d2c/Parser/Parser.Json.cs#L47) defined with parser combinators which is almost in step translation from Haskell code.

If we see generics as ability to have type level variables, higher-kinded type is ability to define a function on the type level. Of course in a limited way like in Scala, not "the same" function like in Idris.
https://gist.github.com/tgrospic/661f6504c4940ac6b15e13c06abbdffe
Lightweight higher-kinded polymorphism paper describes how with a technique of defunctionalization, functions can be encoded into a first-order language (type level C#). Similar how predicate functions are encoded in Mongo query or GraphQL (filter, sort, ...).

I'd be happy to hear anyone's opinion. Cheers!

> Well it's not because `F<A>` is has kind `*` when `F` has kind `* -> *`. And we cannot use kind `*` in generics position.

Yes, but no. I probably should have explained that better. The `<F<A>, F<B>>` part just declares generics so F has kind `* -> *` and both `A` and `B` have kind `*`
```csharp
F<A> Foo<F<A>, F<B>>(F<A> fa, F<B> fb)=> fa;
```
would be just a syntactic sugar for
```csharp
F<A> Foo<F, A, B>(F<A> fa, F<B> fb) where F : <> => fa;
```
so that it can be called like this
```csharp
var foo = Foo(fa, fb);
```

With  `<F, A, B>` syntax it's technically possible to infer all the types and call it with `Foo(fa, fb);`
but it'd break code that uses `Foo<A, B>(A fa, B fb)` so it can't be done as explained here https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/5023#issuecomment-170154313

just like `Foo<F<NotGonnaUseIt_A>>()`? But `Foo<F<>>()` might be better
